points_json.example: A man who slept 2 hours a night for a week, spent his family's savings on 3 cars, and believes he is about to become a famous inventor.
points_json.point: Bipolar I Disorder needs at least one manic episode — a week or more of abnormally high energy, little need for sleep, racing thoughts, fast talking, risky behavior, and grandiosity. Depressive episodes usually happen too, but one manic episode alone is enough for the diagnosis.

points_json.example: Remember DIGFAST: Distractibility, Indiscretion (risky acts), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep loss, Talkativeness.
points_json.point: A manic episode has 3+ of these (4 if mood is only irritable): inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, less need for sleep, more talkative than usual, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and risky behavior like wild spending or unsafe sex.

points_json.example: A woman who for 4 days feels unusually cheerful, needs only 4 hours of sleep, and starts 5 new projects — but still goes to work and functions.
points_json.point: Hypomania is a milder, shorter version of mania — at least 4 days of elevated mood and energy that others notice, but without severe life damage or psychosis. Bipolar II Disorder means at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode. Bipolar II is NOT milder overall — its depressions are often severe.

points_json.example: A student who for 2 years swings between mildly high energy weeks and mildly low weeks, never fully stable, never fully ill.
points_json.point: Cyclothymic Disorder is a chronic, milder swinging — at least 2 years (1 year in youth) of hypomanic-like and depressive-like symptoms that never meet full criteria for mania or major depression, yet never disappear for more than 2 months.

points_json.example: A bipolar patient who during depression cannot get out of bed, then months later during mania gives away money to strangers.
points_json.point: Depressive episodes in bipolar look like regular major depression — sadness, no energy, no pleasure, sleep and appetite changes. But treating bipolar depression with antidepressants alone can trigger mania, so mood stabilizers are essential.

points_json.example: If one identical twin has bipolar disorder, the other twin's risk is 60–80% — among the highest heritability of any mental disorder.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics are very strong, plus brain chemistry (norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine imbalance), disrupted circadian rhythms, stressful life events that trigger episodes, and sometimes medical causes like thyroid problems or steroid medicines.

points_json.example: A patient on lithium gets regular blood tests and stays episode-free for 3 years.
points_json.point: Treatment: mood stabilizers are the foundation — lithium is the classic choice (needs blood monitoring), valproate and lamotrigine are common alternatives. Antipsychotics help mania, and psychotherapy (psychoeducation, keeping regular sleep routines) prevents relapse. Stopping medicine is the top trigger for new episodes.

points_json.example: A rapid-cycling patient has 6 distinct mood episodes in one year — mania, depression, mania again.
points_json.point: Course specifiers: rapid cycling means 4+ mood episodes in a year (harder to treat), mixed features means manic and depressive symptoms together, and episodes can include psychotic features like delusions of grandeur during mania.

summary: Mood swings between extreme highs and deep lows. This note covers Bipolar I, Bipolar II, cyclothymia, manic symptoms, causes, and treatments in simple words.
title: Bipolar and Related Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A 16-year-old girl who weighs 35 kg but cries daily believing she is fat, and runs 2 hours every morning to burn every calorie.
points_json.point: Anorexia Nervosa means severely restricting food, an intense fear of gaining weight, and a distorted body image — the person sees fat where there is none. It has the highest death rate of any mental disorder, from starvation or suicide. Two types: restricting (just dieting/fasting/exercise) and binge-eating/purging.

points_json.example: A college student who eats 5,000 calories alone at midnight, then vomits in the bathroom and brushes her teeth so nobody knows.
points_json.point: Bulimia Nervosa means repeated binge eating (eating huge amounts with loss of control) followed by purging — vomiting, laxatives, or extreme exercise — at least once a week for 3 months. Unlike anorexia, weight is usually normal, so the disorder stays hidden.

points_json.example: A man who eats an entire pizza, a tub of ice cream, and chips in one sitting twice a week, then feels deep shame — but never purges.
points_json.point: Binge-Eating Disorder is the most common eating disorder — regular binge episodes with distress and shame, but no purging or extreme dieting afterward. It is linked with obesity and depression.

points_json.example: A 7-year-old who eats only white rice and plain bread, and gags at any new food.
points_json.point: ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) means avoiding food from sensory issues, fear of choking, or no interest in eating — causing weight loss or nutrition problems, but without body-image distortion. Common in children and autistic youth.

points_json.example: A pregnant woman who craves and eats chalk and clay daily.
points_json.point: Pica is eating non-food items (clay, chalk, paper) for a month or more. Rumination Disorder is repeatedly bringing food back up and re-chewing it. Both need medical checks first — pica can signal iron deficiency.

points_json.example: A perfectionist teenager whose whole family diets and whose social media is full of thin ideal images.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, perfectionist and anxious temperament, cultural pressure for thinness, family focus on weight, dieting (the top trigger for anorexia), and trauma. Sports like gymnastics and modeling carry higher risk.

points_json.example: In family-based treatment, parents temporarily take charge of all meals until their teenager's weight is restored.
points_json.point: Treatments: for teens with anorexia, family-based treatment (parents refeed the child) works best. CBT-E (enhanced CBT) is the top therapy for bulimia and binge-eating disorder. SSRIs help bulimia. Hospitalization is needed when weight or electrolytes become dangerous.

points_json.example: A recovered bulimia patient eats 3 planned meals plus snacks daily — no skipping, which was her main binge trigger.
points_json.point: Recovery skills: regular eating patterns (skipping meals triggers binges), challenging body-checking habits, building identity beyond appearance, and treating co-occurring anxiety or depression.

summary: When the relationship with food and body turns dangerous. This note covers anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating disorder, ARFID, causes, and treatments in simple words.
title: Eating Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A 9-year-old who loses his homework daily, cannot sit through a meal, and blurts answers before the teacher finishes the question.
points_json.point: ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) has two symptom groups: inattention (careless mistakes, disorganization, forgetfulness, losing things) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (fidgeting, cannot stay seated, excessive talking, interrupting). Symptoms must appear before age 12 and in 2+ settings like home and school.

points_json.example: An inattentive girl stares out the window all lesson (missed diagnosis for years). A hyperactive boy runs around the classroom.
points_json.point: Three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined. Girls more often show the quiet inattentive type and get diagnosed late. ADHD continues into adulthood for most — adults show restlessness, poor time management, and impulsive decisions.

points_json.example: A 4-year-old who does not respond to his name, avoids eye contact, lines up toy cars for hours, and screams if the routine changes.
points_json.point: Autism Spectrum Disorder has two core areas: persistent problems with social communication (eye contact, conversation, friendships) plus restricted, repetitive behaviors (routines, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities). It is a spectrum — from people needing full-time support to highly verbal individuals.

points_json.example: An autistic boy who covers his ears and cries at the sound of a hand dryer.
points_json.point: Sensory differences are part of autism — over-sensitivity (sounds, lights, textures feel painful) or under-sensitivity (seeking spinning, pressure). Special interests can be deep and joyful, like memorizing every train schedule.

points_json.example: A child who at age 5 speaks in single words and needs help with dressing and eating.
points_json.point: Intellectual Developmental Disorder (intellectual disability) means significantly below-average intellectual functioning plus problems with adaptive skills (communication, self-care, daily living), starting in childhood. Severity ranges from mild to profound.

points_json.example: Twin and family studies show ADHD and autism are among the most heritable conditions — genes matter more than parenting.
points_json.point: Causes: strong genetics for all three, plus prenatal factors (mother's smoking/alcohol, premature birth, low birth weight). Parenting style does NOT cause ADHD or autism — that old myth is fully disproven.

points_json.example: A child on stimulant medicine sits through class for the first time and finishes his worksheet.
points_json.point: ADHD treatment: stimulant medicines (methylphenidate) are the most effective, plus behavioral parent training and classroom support. Autism treatment: early behavioral intervention, speech and occupational therapy, and support for families — there is no cure, the goal is skills and quality of life.

points_json.example: An autistic teenager thrives with noise-cancelling headphones, a visual daily schedule, and a teacher who lets him take movement breaks.
points_json.point: Support that helps: structured routines, clear visual instructions, sensory accommodations, social skills groups, and celebrating strengths — many autistic and ADHD people have remarkable creativity, focus, and honesty.

summary: Conditions that begin in childhood and shape how the brain develops. This note covers ADHD, autism, and intellectual disability — symptoms, causes, and support — in simple words.
title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders: ADHD and Autism (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A woman who lies awake until 3 AM every night for months, then drags through work exhausted and dreads bedtime.
points_json.point: Insomnia Disorder means trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early — at least 3 nights a week for 3 months — with daytime tiredness and poor functioning. It is the most common sleep disorder, and stress, screens, and irregular schedules fuel it.

points_json.example: A student who suddenly collapses laughing during a joke, then wakes up minutes later confused.
points_json.point: Narcolepsy means the brain cannot control sleep-wake properly: sudden irresistible sleep attacks in the daytime plus cataplexy (muscles going limp with strong emotions like laughter). It is caused by loss of hypocretin, a brain chemical that keeps us awake.

points_json.example: A man whose wife says he snores loudly, gasps, and stops breathing many times each night, then falls asleep at his desk daily.
points_json.point: Obstructive Sleep Apnea is repeated breathing pauses during sleep when the throat closes — causing loud snoring, gasping, and daytime sleepiness. It raises blood pressure and heart risk, and weight loss plus CPAP machines (night breathing masks) treat it.

points_json.example: A child who sits up screaming in the first hours of sleep, eyes open but unresponsive, and remembers nothing in the morning.
points_json.point: Parasomnias: sleepwalking and sleep terrors happen in deep sleep (the person is confused and forgets it), while nightmare disorder and REM sleep behavior disorder (acting out dreams, like punching while dreaming of a fight) happen in dream sleep.

points_json.example: An elderly man who kicks and shouts in his sleep, sometimes falling out of bed while dreaming he is being chased.
points_json.point: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder is especially important — the body fails to stay still during dreams, so people act dreams out. In older adults it can be an early sign of Parkinson's disease.

points_json.example: A woman whose legs tingle and crawl every evening, forcing her to walk around instead of sleeping.
points_json.point: Restless Legs Syndrome is an irresistible urge to move the legs with uncomfortable creeping sensations, worse at rest and at night. Iron deficiency is a common cause — check iron levels first.

points_json.example: A chronic insomniac learns to use the bed only for sleep, gets up when awake 20 minutes, and stops all screens an hour before bed — sleeping better in 3 weeks without pills.
points_json.point: CBT-I (CBT for insomnia) beats sleeping pills long-term: stimulus control (bed = sleep only), sleep restriction (temporarily less time in bed to rebuild sleep pressure), and fixing worry thoughts about sleep. Good sleep hygiene — dark cool room, fixed wake time, no caffeine after noon — helps everyone.

points_json.example: A night-shift nurse who sleeps with blackout curtains, earplugs, and a strict daytime sleep schedule.
points_json.point: Shift workers and teens with delayed sleep phase need light therapy and strict schedules. Sleeping pills help short-term but cause dependence — they are a bridge, not a solution.

summary: When sleep itself becomes the problem. This note covers insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea, parasomnias, and proven sleep treatments in simple words.
title: Sleep-Wake Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A woman with mild back pain who has visited 12 doctors, had 5 scans, and spends hours daily researching diseases online.
points_json.point: Somatic Symptom Disorder means the person has distressing physical symptoms (pain, fatigue) plus excessive thoughts, worry, and time spent on them — doctor-shopping, constant health Googling. The symptoms are real to the person, even when medical tests find little.

points_json.example: A healthy 25-year-old who is convinced every headache is a brain tumor and checks his body for lumps 20 times a day.
points_json.point: Illness Anxiety Disorder (the new name for hypochondriasis) is intense fear of having a serious disease with little or no actual symptoms. The person misreads normal body sensations as deadly illness and seeks constant reassurance.

points_json.example: A woman who suddenly cannot move her legs after a family fight — all scans are normal, and the paralysis fades once the conflict is resolved.
points_json.point: Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) means real neurological symptoms — paralysis, blindness, seizures — with no medical cause. It often follows stress or trauma, and the person is not faking; the brain genuinely produces the symptom.

points_json.example: A hospital patient who secretly injects herself with bacteria to stay admitted and receive care and sympathy.
points_json.point: Factitious Disorder is deliberately faking illness — even harming oneself — to play the sick role and get care. Imposed on another (by proxy) is when a caregiver makes a child or elder sick for attention. This is different from malingering.

points_json.example: A man who fakes back pain to get insurance money and time off work.
points_json.point: Malingering is NOT a mental disorder — it is faking symptoms for a clear external reward like money, drugs, or avoiding duty. The difference from factitious disorder: malingering has an obvious outside gain.

points_json.example: A child who learned that stomach aches get her out of scary school days.
points_json.point: Causes: the sick role can bring care and escape from duties (reinforcement), anxious temperament, childhood illness or trauma, and cultural ways of expressing distress through the body — very common worldwide.

points_json.example: A somatic symptom patient learns that her stomach pain spikes with stress, and practices relaxation instead of rushing to the emergency room.
points_json.point: Treatment: regular scheduled doctor visits (not emergency visits), CBT to challenge illness fears, stress management, and treating co-occurring anxiety or depression. Reassurance alone never works — the worry always returns.

summary: When distress speaks through the body. This note covers somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety, conversion disorder, and factitious disorder in simple words.
title: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A woman who cannot remember her wedding day or her children's births, though her other memories are fine.
points_json.point: Dissociation means the mind disconnects — from memory, identity, or surroundings. Dissociative Amnesia is inability to recall important personal information (usually after trauma) that is too big for normal forgetting. With dissociative fugue, the person also wanders away and may start a new identity.

points_json.example: A student who after a car accident feels like she is watching herself from outside her body, as if in a movie.
points_json.point: Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder: depersonalization is feeling detached from your own body or thoughts (like an outside observer); derealization is feeling the world is unreal, foggy, or dreamlike. The person knows it is strange, which makes it scarier.

points_json.example: A woman who finds clothes she never bought, gets called by a different name by strangers, and loses hours of time.
points_json.point: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID, formerly multiple personality) means two or more distinct identity states take control, with gaps in memory. It is strongly linked to severe, repeated childhood trauma — the mind's extreme defense was to split.

points_json.example: A soldier who during battle felt he floated above his body watching himself fight.
points_json.point: Dissociation often starts as a survival trick — during overwhelming trauma, the mind detaches to endure the unendurable. Peritraumatic dissociation (during the trauma) predicts later PTSD.

points_json.example: A DID patient in therapy slowly maps her identity states and learns they all formed to protect a hurt child.
points_json.point: Controversy note: DID is debated — most experts see it as a real trauma disorder, while some argue therapy can accidentally shape symptoms. Careful diagnosis matters, and the trauma link is well-supported.

points_json.example: A depersonalization patient practices grounding: naming 5 things she can see, 4 she can touch, 3 she can hear.
points_json.point: Treatment: trauma-focused psychotherapy is the core — processing the underlying trauma, grounding techniques for detachment episodes, and building safety. There is no specific medicine for dissociation itself; medicines treat co-occurring anxiety or depression.

points_json.example: A fugue patient found 200 km from home with no memory of traveling there — police help him contact family, and memories return gradually.
points_json.point: For dissociative amnesia and fugue, most memories return on their own once the person is safe. Hypnosis or medicine-assisted interviews are rarely needed and must be done carefully to avoid false memories.

summary: When the mind disconnects to survive. This note covers dissociative amnesia, depersonalization, and dissociative identity disorder in simple words.
title: Dissociative Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A man who needs a drink every morning to stop shaking, has lost his job, but keeps drinking despite his wife's pleas.
points_json.point: Substance Use Disorder is diagnosed from 11 criteria — using more than planned, failed attempts to quit, cravings, neglecting duties, social problems, dangerous use, tolerance (needing more), and withdrawal. Severity: 2–3 = mild, 4–5 = moderate, 6+ = severe.

points_json.example: A college student who planned to study but spent the whole weekend drinking and missed Monday's exam.
points_json.point: Key criteria explained: loss of control (using longer than intended), time swallowed by the substance, giving up hobbies and friends, and continuing despite knowing it causes depression, liver damage, or family fights.

points_json.example: A daily drinker who sweats, shakes, and sees things when he tries to stop for a day.
points_json.point: Tolerance means needing bigger doses for the same effect. Withdrawal means the body revolts without the substance — alcohol withdrawal can be deadly (seizures), opioid withdrawal feels like severe flu, and nicotine withdrawal brings irritability and cravings.

points_json.example: Ten classes: alcohol, cannabis, hallucinogens, inhalants, opioids, sedatives, stimulants (cocaine, meth), tobacco, caffeine, and others.
points_json.point: DSM-5-TR covers 10 substance classes. Each can cause use disorder, intoxication, and withdrawal (caffeine has no use disorder diagnosis, but withdrawal — headaches, fatigue — is real).

points_json.example: A gambler who has lost his house, borrows from loan sharks, and lies to his family — but has never touched drugs.
points_json.point: Gambling Disorder is the only behavioral addiction in DSM-5-TR — the same craving, loss of control, and life damage as drug addiction, without any substance. Internet gaming disorder is listed as needing more study.

points_json.example: A teenager whose friends all vape is far more likely to start than one whose friends don't.
points_json.point: Risk factors: genetics (addiction runs in families), early first use, peer pressure, trauma and mental illness (people self-medicate anxiety or depression), and easy availability.

points_json.example: A smoker quits using nicotine patches plus a support group — combining medicine and counseling doubles success.
points_json.point: Treatment: detox for dangerous withdrawals (alcohol, sedatives), medicines (methadone or buprenorphine for opioids, naltrexone for alcohol, nicotine replacement for smoking), CBT and motivational interviewing, and support groups. Relapse is common — it is part of recovery, not failure.

points_json.example: A recovering alcoholic avoids wedding parties for a year, practices saying no, and calls his sponsor when cravings hit.
points_json.point: Recovery skills: avoiding triggers, building a substance-free social circle, treating co-occurring depression or anxiety, and long-term follow-up. Harm reduction (clean needles, not driving drunk) saves lives even before full recovery.

summary: When use becomes dependence. This note covers substance use disorder criteria, all 10 substance classes, gambling disorder, and treatments in simple words.
title: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: An elderly man with fever who suddenly does not recognize his daughter and thinks he is in his childhood home — but was fine yesterday.
points_json.point: Delirium is a sudden, fluctuating confusion — inattention, disorientation, sometimes hallucinations — caused by a medical problem like infection, dehydration, or new medicine. It comes on in hours or days. Unlike dementia, delirium is usually reversible if the cause is treated.

points_json.example: A grandmother who keeps asking the same question every 10 minutes and gets lost in her own street.
points_json.point: Major Neurocognitive Disorder (dementia) is a gradual, lasting decline in memory, thinking, or daily skills that steals independence. Mild neurocognitive disorder is the earlier stage — problems are noticeable but the person still manages daily life.

points_json.example: A retired teacher who forgets recent conversations, repeats stories, and later cannot name common objects.
points_json.point: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause — it starts with short-term memory loss (new memories don't stick) and slowly takes language, judgment, and personality. Brain plaques and tangles are the hallmark; genetics (APOE4 gene) raises risk.

points_json.example: A man whose thinking worsens in clear steps — each small stroke drops him to a new, lower level.
points_json.point: Vascular neurocognitive disorder follows strokes — decline happens in steps, not smoothly. Lewy body disease brings vivid visual hallucinations and Parkinson-like stiffness. Frontotemporal disease changes personality first (rudeness, apathy) while memory stays longer.

points_json.example: A daughter who labels every drawer, keeps a fixed daily routine, and plays old songs her father loves.
points_json.point: Care that helps: structured routines, labeled surroundings, gentle reorientation, music and familiar faces, treating depression (common in dementia), and supporting exhausted caregivers — caregiver stress is a huge, hidden part of the illness.

points_json.example: A 70-year-old who walks daily, controls blood pressure, and does crosswords has a lower dementia risk than his inactive peers.
points_json.point: Prevention: what protects the heart protects the brain — exercise, blood pressure control, no smoking, diabetes control, social activity, and lifelong learning. Hearing loss treatment also lowers risk.

points_json.example: A patient whose confusion vanished 2 days after antibiotics cured his urinary infection.
points_json.point: Always rule out reversible causes first: infections, dehydration, vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid problems, depression (which can mimic dementia), and medicine side effects. Treating these can fully restore thinking.

points_json.example: Newer medicines slow Alzheimer's slightly in early stages but do not cure it; most drugs manage symptoms like agitation or sleep problems.
points_json.point: Treatment reality: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) help mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's modestly. The main work is care planning — safety (stoves, driving, wandering), legal arrangements, and family support.

summary: When memory and thinking fade. This note covers delirium, Alzheimer's, vascular and Lewy body dementia, prevention, and care in simple words.
title: Neurocognitive Disorders (DSM-5-TR)
